segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Today, we’ll be continuing the series of lectures on memory by focusing on what is called episodic memory and what can happen if this is not working properly.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Episodic memory refers to the memory of an event or ‘episode’.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Episodic memories allow us to mentally travel back in time to an event from the past.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Episodic memories include various details about these events, for example, when an event happened and other information such as the location [[ ]] .

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: To help understand this concept, try to remember the last time you ate dinner at a restaurant.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The ability to remember where you ate, who you were with and the items you ordered are all features of an episodic memory.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Episodic memory is distinct from another type of memory called semantic memory.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This is the type of factual memory that we have in common with everyone else – that is your general knowledge of the world [[ ]] .

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: To build upon a previous example, remembering where you parked your car is an example of episodic memory, but your understanding of what a car is and how an engine works are examples of sematic memory.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Unlike episodic memory, semantic memory isn’t dependent on recalling personal experiences. [[ ]] Episodic memory can be thought of as a process with several different steps of memory processing: encoding, consolidation and retrieval.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The initial step is called encoding.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This involves the process of receiving and registering information, which is necessary for creating memories of information or events that you experience.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The degree to which you can successfully encode information depends on the level of attention you give to an event while it’s actually happening [[ ]] .

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Being distracted can make effective encoding very difficult.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Encoding of episodic memories is also influenced by how you process the event.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: For example, if you were introduced to someone called Charlie, you might make the connection that your uncle has the same name.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Future recollection of Charlie’s name is much easier if you have a strategy to help you encode it. [[ ]] Memory consolidation, the next step in forming an episodic memory, is the process by which memories of encoded information are strengthened, stabilised and stored to facilitate later retrieval.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Consolidation is most effective when the information being stored can be linked to an existing network of information [[ ]] .

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Consolidation makes it possible for you to store memories for later retrieval indefinitely.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Forming strong memories depends on the frequency with which you try to retrieve them [[ ]] .

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Memories can fade or become harder to retrieve if they aren’t used very often.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The last step in forming episodic memories is called retrieval, which is the conscious recollection of encoded information.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Retrieving information from episodic memory depends upon semantic, olfactory, auditory and visual factors.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: These help episodic memory retrieval by acting as a prompt.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: For example, when recalling where you parked your car you may use the colour of a sign close to where you parked [[ ]] .

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: You actually have to mentally travel back to the moment you parked. —————— There are a wide range of neurological diseases and conditions that can affect episodic memory.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: These range from Alzheimer’s to schizophrenia to autism.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: An impairment of episodic memory can have a profound effect on individuals’ lives.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: For example, the symptoms of schizophrenia can be reasonably well controlled by medication; however, patients’ episodic memory may still be impaired and so they are often unable to return to university or work.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Recent studies have shown that computer- assisted games designed to keep the brain active can help improve their episodic memory. [[ ]] Episodic memories can help people connect with others, for instance by sharing intimate details about their past; something individuals with autism often have problems with.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This may be caused by an absence of a sense of self [[ ]] .

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This is essential for the storage of episodic memory, and has been found to be impaired in children with autism.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Research has shown that treatments that improve memory may also have a positive impact on children’s social development.
